steps.action:
# The Last Watch

Maren had kept the light for thirty-one years, and in all that time the sea had never once asked her permission before taking something.

It had taken her husband first, then her dog, then — slowly, the way the tide erodes a cliff rather than collapses it — her certainty that the world beyond the rocks was worth warning ships about.

Still, every evening at dusk she climbed the iron stairs. Seventy-two steps. She had stopped counting around year four, and started again around year twenty, when counting became the thing that got her to the top.

One November a freighter ignored the light entirely — she watched it move with stupid confidence through the fog — and drove itself onto the shoal with a sound like a cathedral falling. She rowed out alone in the dark and pulled three men from the water. They were young and shaking and one of them wept openly, which she found she didn't mind at all.

They stayed four days waiting for rescue. She fed them fish stew and taught them a card game her husband had invented, with rules that changed depending on the direction of the wind.

When they finally left, the youngest one stopped at the dock and looked up at the tower.

"Don't you get lonely?" he asked.

Maren considered the question seriously, the way it deserved.

"The light doesn't," she said.

She went back inside. At dusk, she climbed the stairs.
